meta.subtitle: What was proposed, what the user decided, what shipped, and what's still open
meta.summary: Live decision log. Original proposal sections preserved with a status callout marking what the user decided and where each decision stands in implementation. Companion research (chart syntax landscape + visualization catalogue gap analysis) summarised at the top; full reports in notes/.

blocks.title: Where we are
blocks.summary: Five of six decisions answered, three shipped, two pending. Library adoption deferred. Research landed and recommends Vega-Lite as the syntactic baseline for the type-unification work.
bullets: **Shipped:** code → output label rename, function-grouped chart picker, smart-quiet table chrome (notebook feel — opacity 0.15 default, 1.0 on hover / focus / active state).

**Decided, not yet built:** chart-type unification — canonical types (`plot` / `arc` / `bar+mode`) with old type names kept as desugaring aliases that authors can still override per-property. Per the syntax research, the shape follows Vega-Lite's mark-composition pattern.

**Decided, not actionable yet:** no new chart libraries this round. Current SVG renderer stays. Library swaps revisited only after unification (we'll know the canonical shapes we'd want a library to render).
**Newly raised by the user:** runtime chart-type toggle — when data shape allows, let the reader flip between line / area / bar from the chart itself. Separate from unification but enabled by it.

**Research landed:** notes/chart-syntax-research.md (8 libraries surveyed, Vega-Lite recommended), notes/viz-catalog.md (1022 lines, eight sections — six-URL marketing-catalogue gap analysis + datavizcatalogue function taxonomy + D3 gallery + datavizproject.com). 15 visualization gaps and ~50 mode-variations on existing types identified.

blocks.title: Recently shipped
blocks.lead: What landed since the original review.

blocks.content: example-pair right column reads **Output** (was 'Render'). Schema field stays `render` for backwards-compat — no doc churn.

29 chart cards distributed across 8 function groups: Compare values · Show change over time · Show distribution · Show parts of a whole · Show relationships · Show hierarchy · Show flow or movement · Show location. Each card keeps its live tiny render + #anchor jump.

Table controls at opacity 0.15 by default. Reveal on hover or keyboard focus. Force-show via `:has()` when filter has text, any chip is active, or view is non-default. Charts and code blocks were already hover-only.

Canonical types: `plot` (with `marks: [dots|line|area]`), `arc` (with `mode: pie|donut` + `arc: {start, end}` + `inner_radius`), `bar` (with `mode: single|stacked|grouped`). Legacy names (scatter / line / area / pie / donut / stacked-bar / grouped-bar) keep working as aliases that desugar to the canonical form with appropriate defaults — and author overrides win over alias presets. Verified: all 6 canonical+alias Cartesian forms produce matching DOM, donut+pie+arc-override all render correctly, all 29 existing chart types still pass regression tests.

blocks.title: Research findings (this session)
blocks.lead: Two reports landed; both inform the pending work.

blocks.content: Full report: `notes/chart-syntax-research.md`. Surveyed eight libraries — Vega-Lite, Observable Plot, D3, ECharts, Plotly, Highcharts, Chart.js, Apache Superset. The recommendation is **Vega-Lite as the syntactic baseline** for our unification: its `mark: [...]` composition pattern is the closest analogue to `type: plot, marks: [...]`, and its encoding model handles cross-shape rendering (same data, different mark) cleanly.

blocks.title: What we should take from Vega-Lite
blocks.content: The mark-composition model and the principle that 'a chart is data + encoding + mark', not 'a chart is a top-level type'. The reader writes the data once and switches marks to switch chart shapes — that maps directly to the user's runtime-toggle idea (decision 6).

blocks.title: What we should NOT take
blocks.content: Vega-Lite's depth — selection signals, layered transforms, complex `encoding.color.condition` blocks. These shrink AI emission's success rate. Keep the surface flat: data + marks + a small property bag per mark.

Full report: `notes/viz-catalog.md` (1022 lines, eight sections). Cross-references oku's 29 chart types against six marketing catalogues + the D3 gallery + datavizcatalogue's function taxonomy + datavizproject.com's ~150-type reference.

rows: Master list + 15 gaps + 10 improvements to existing types. Highlights pictograms, marimekko, density plot, candlestick, sunburst, stream graph, violin, dot plot, error-bar.
Eight function categories that drove the new picker grouping. Recommends hybrid (function primary, family secondary) — shipped in B.
20 new candidates (beeswarm, contour, sunburst, sankey-with-cycles, etc.) + 15 interactivity techniques worth lifting (zoom-to-region, brush-to-filter, lasso-select, force-relax, click-to-fix-node).

10 distinct new candidates + 51 named variations of existing oku types that could become `mode:` switches post-unification (radial-bar, 100%-stacked, marimekko-as-stacked-bar-with-scaled-widths, etc.).

blocks.title: Top-priority new visualizations (synthesised across all four sources)
blocks.content: **Sunburst** (hierarchy alternative to treemap), **Violin** (distribution alternative to box-plot), **Marimekko** (variable-width stacked bar — earns a `mode` on bar), **Density plot / KDE** (smoothed histogram), **Candlestick** (financial OHLC, distinct shape), **Stream graph** (alternative stacked area), **Dot plot** (one-axis comparison), **Beeswarm** (jittered scatter for one-axis distribution). Eight items — discuss before adding.

blocks.title: The north star
blocks.lead: Restate the contract so every later decision is measured against it. (Unchanged from the original review.)

blocks.title: Contract (from the user, paraphrased)
blocks.content: JSON is the substrate so AI can read / write / modify content without fighting style or glue markup. The presentation should be capable yet simple — simplicity is the ultimate sophistication. Pre-defined structures should be enough for the 90% case, but raw HTML/JS escape hatches should remain available for the 10%.

Two failure modes to guard against. **Drift toward complexity:** every new feature adds schema surface, runtime branches, and visual-language vocabulary the reader has to learn. Each addition is locally justifiable; collectively they erode the contract. **Drift toward purity:** rejecting every addition leaves the reader with bullet-points and tables for everything a chart could illustrate. Equally a failure.

The discipline: every new primitive must answer two questions. **(1) Can AI emit this in one obvious shape, with no per-page judgement calls?** (2) Does the rendered result earn the schema cost — i.e., does the reader recognise the shape faster than they'd parse a paragraph + bullets?

blocks.title: Unify the bar family
blocks.lead: Three chart types today differ only in how multi-series rows render. Collapse to one with a mode switch.

blocks.title: Decision: Yes — alias desugar (Status: shipped)
blocks.content: `type: bar` is canonical with `mode: single | stacked | grouped`. `stacked-bar` / `grouped-bar` keep working as aliases that desugar to `bar, mode: stacked|grouped`. Author can override any preset on the alias form. No backward-compat break — all existing pages pass regression tests.

AI picks one shape (`type: bar`) and answers one question (`mode`). Single-series omits `mode` (defaults to `single`); both series-modes share the same `categories` + `series` shape. Post-unification, the bar `mode` enum can widen to absorb research-recommended variants (marimekko = variable-width stacked, percent-stacked, radial-bar).

blocks.title: Unify scatter / line / area
blocks.lead: Same axes, same data shape, different mark.

blocks.title: Decision: Yes — alias desugar (Status: shipped)
blocks.content: `type: plot` is canonical with `marks: [dots | line | area]`. `scatter` / `line` / `area` keep working as aliases. Author can override marks on either form. Mark-composition matches Vega-Lite. Verified: all 6 canonical+alias Cartesian forms produce identical dots/lines/areas counts.

blocks.title: Enabler for decision 6 (runtime type-toggle)
blocks.content: Once data + axes are decoupled from mark choice, the chart can offer the reader an inline picker: switch the SAME chart between dots / line / area / bar at runtime by mutating `marks` and re-rendering. The data shape doesn't change, the encoding does. This is the Vega-Lite pattern.

blocks.title: Unify donut / pie / gauge
blocks.lead: Three primitives that share an arc-geometry renderer.

blocks.title: Decision: Yes for pie+donut, no for gauge (Status: shipped)
blocks.content: `type: arc` is canonical for pie + donut. `pie` and `donut` stay as aliases, with `arc: { start, end }` and `inner_radius` overridable on either. Verified: `type: pie + arc.end=270` produces a 3/4 pie; `type: donut + inner_radius=0.3` produces a thicker ring. Gauge stays its own type — different data shape (value + zones).

blocks.title: Future addition (post-unification)
blocks.content: **Sunburst** — a multi-level radial hierarchy chart — fits naturally as `type: arc, levels: [...]` where each level adds an outer ring. Surfaced by the visualization-catalogue research as a top-priority gap. Implement once the arc renderer is unified.

blocks.title: Interaction budget — smart hiding, no settings
blocks.lead: Capable yet quiet — notebook feel. No new toggle.

blocks.title: Decision: smart defaults, no setting (Status: partial — table chrome shipped, more surfaces pending)
blocks.content: User explicitly rejected an `interaction_density` switch. Default behaviour should cover both worlds — surfaces stay quiet until the reader intends to use them (hover / focus / non-default state). The system should feel like a well-designed notebook: present but not distracting.

rows: Table controls (filter / chips / group-by / view / expand)
opacity 0.15 default; 1.0 on hover/focus; force-show via `:has()` when filter has text or any chip active or view non-default.

Earlier polish locked it as a flush corner label. A regression test forbids hover state. Future trim: only render when the block sits inside a multi-language sequence — needs chrome.js detection, not pure CSS.
Fold detection skipped on blocks under 8 lines. Short blocks no longer add gutter chevrons — a 3-line shell command stays clean.

Drag handle resting state is a 2px bar in `--border-soft`; widens to 20px on hover and brightens to `--accent-strong`. Reviewed in this round and judged already at the right level — further fade would make it undiscoverable.

blocks.title: Runtime chart-type toggle (new decision)
blocks.lead: User raised this mid-stream: when data shape allows, let the reader switch chart type in-place.

blocks.title: Decision: under design — gated on type unification (task C) landing first
blocks.content: Same data shape can drive multiple chart shapes. Line / area / scatter all consume `series of {x, y}` — flipping among them is a mark change, not a data change. Bar/column from the same `{x, y}` set is also valid (treating x as category). The user wants a UI control that lets the reader pick — useful both for comparison ('does this look like a trend or a series of points?') and for accommodating a reader's mental-model preference.

Implementation shape (proposal): once `type: plot` is canonical (task C), every chart gains an optional `compatible_with: [...]` list of alternative marks. When non-empty, the chart toolbar grows a mark-picker dropdown alongside the existing download / view-data / expand buttons. Switching the picker mutates the live `marks` array and re-renders in place — same x-axis, same data points, different visual encoding. Hover-stickiness handled the same way as today's view-switch on tables (the picker only appears on the chart's hover/focus, per the smart-hide principle).

blocks.title: What it needs first
blocks.content: Task C must land before this is implementable. The toggle relies on the canonical `marks` axis existing; until then there's nothing to swap between.

blocks.title: Library adoption
blocks.lead: Honest cost / benefit per candidate. The earlier review's recommendation stands — no new libraries this round.

blocks.title: Decision: defer all (Status: decided)
blocks.content: Library adoption pays off once we know the unified shapes — then we can ask 'does library X render this shape better than our renderer?' instead of asking 'should we use X?' in the abstract. Until then, the existing SVG renderer wins on control + predictability + zero bundle weight.

rows: **Defer.** Imposes its own data-binding model. Less code per chart, more cognitive shift per chart.
**Watch.** Mark-composition aligns with our unification but it owns SVG output → we'd lose hover/pin/cursor control.
**Watch — syntactic inspiration, not runtime.** Take the schema shape (mark composition), not the runtime.
**Keep.** Each earns its weight on a distinct problem (diagrams / highlighting / search).

blocks.title: Decision: Use code + output (Status: shipped)
blocks.content: example-pair right column reads **Output** (was 'Render'); left column reads **Code** (was 'Source'). The schema fields stay `code` and `render` for backwards-compat — only the visible labels changed.

blocks.title: Pick by function (was: Pick by family)
blocks.lead: Group the 29 chart variants by what the author is trying to say.

blocks.title: Decision: group by function (Status: shipped)
blocks.content: Eight function groups, hybrid model — function as the primary picker axis, family kept as secondary in the lower sections. Labels follow the datavizcatalogue function taxonomy, lightly edited for plainer wording.

blocks.title: Risk register (updated)
blocks.lead: What could go wrong with the pending work.

rows: Existing pages emit `scatter` / `line` / `area` / `stacked-bar` / `grouped-bar` / `pie` / `donut`. If aliases break, all 18 doc pages fail to render.

Aliases are non-negotiable, not optional. Test matrix: every old type name must produce the same DOM as before. Schema accepts both old and new; renderer normalises. Tests: existing chart-content regression tests already cover this surface.
Reader switches to a mark the data doesn't actually support (e.g. line on categorical x).
`compatible_with` is author-declared, not auto-inferred. Author opts in only when they've checked the data shape. UI hides the toggle when only one option exists.
Hidden chrome makes affordances undiscoverable — first-time visitors don't know there's a filter input on the table.
Default opacity is 0.15, not 0. Affordance is visible but quiet — a hint, not a hide. Force-show on active state means the user never loses sight of state they've already set.
Each new chart type expands the schema and the runtime. Adding all 15 from the gap list would re-introduce the drift the north star guards against.

Add one at a time, each with a written justification against the two north-star questions. Sunburst is high-value (different hierarchy view); pictograms are low-value (a styling variant of waffle). Discriminate.
